stories.headline: Can Nifty, Sensex rally further or will bears reign in? 5 factors to steer market this week
stories.title: Can Nifty, Sensex rally further or will bears reign in? 5 factors to steer market this week
stories.summary: Benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty extended gains for a second consecutive session on Friday. Continued strength in IT stocks, which rose for a fourth straight session, along with buying in auto, metal and PSU banking stocks, supported the rally.Looking ahead, the 22,800–22,750 zone remains a crucial support. As long as Nifty sustains above 22,750, the recovery is likely to extend. On the upside, 23,400–23,450 remains the immediate resistance zone, a decisive breakout above which could propel the index towards 23,650, coinciding with its 100-day EMA.Here are 5 factors that investors need to watch out for1.) Q2 earnings - Banking heavyweights HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank all declared their earnings on Saturday. Investors will assess loan growth, deposit mobilisation, margins, asset quality and management commentary for cues on earnings momentum, credit demand and the outlook for the financial sector.India’s largest private lender HDFC Bank on Saturday reported a net profit of Rs 19,510 crore for the second quarter of FY27, marking a 4.6% jump from Rs 18,641 crore posted in the same period last year. HDFC Bank’s net interest income (interest earned less interest expended) for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, grew 9.7% to Rs 34,620 crore from Rs 31,550 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.2.) Oil prices - Crude oil prices climbed sharply higher on Friday to clinch $110 for the first time since May as Iran intensified attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants launched missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine pledged to resume strikes on Russian refineries, fuelling concerns over global energy supplies.Markets remain uncertain about how the conflict will develop. JPMorgan analysts said the war’s eventual trajectory was difficult to model. At the outset, the bank had expected the US administration to avoid crossing certain economic thresholds. Seven months into the conflict, many of those thresholds had been crossed, while a clear exit strategy remained elusive.3.) IT stocks - IT stocks such as TCS, Tech Mahindra, Infosys and Wipro had a strong week, rallying up to 17% and lifting the index by 12% over the week amid better-than-expected earnings and a sharp plunge in AI-linked stocks.Additionally, Nifty IT is firmly placed in the leading quadrant of the RRG, indicating strong relative strength and momentum. On the daily chart, the index is on the cusp of breaking its lower-low, lower-high structure. The 32,000–32,200 zone is the immediate resistance. A decisive and sustained move above this zone could pave the way for a continuation of the pullback in the near term, Sudeep Shah of SBI Securities said.4.) FII activity - Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) remained net sellers for the ninth consecutive week, but outflows eased sharply to Rs 8,991 crore from Rs 30,294 crore in the previous week, according to Bajaj broking.FIIs turned net buyers of Rs 1,166 crore on Friday. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs), meanwhile, remained net buyers for the ninth straight week, with inflows of Rs 7,813 crore, despite net selling of Rs 3,661 crore on Friday. Month-to-date, DII net buying of Rs 48,168 crore has almost entirely offset FII net selling of Rs 48,769 crore.Going ahead, the moderation in FII outflows suggests that market sentiment may be stabilising, although elevated crude oil prices continue to pose a risk to the recovery. Investors will track Brent crude prices and developments in US-Iran relations, while domestic attention will remain on Q2FY27 earnings, Pabitro Mukherjee of Bajaj Broking said.5.) Rupee up for 5th session - The Indian rupee rose 2% this week to record its strongest weekly gain in seven months, supported by policy measures aimed at stabilising the currency. However, analysts cautioned that a sustained recovery would depend on easing the underlying pressures on the rupee.The currency closed at Rs 94.96 per US dollar, up 0.1% on the day, recovering after last week’s slide brought it close to its record low of Rs 96.96 per dollar.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. stories.headline: Starlink: The Promise and the Risk
stories.title: Starlink: The Promise and the Risk
stories.summary: India should welcome new technology, foreign investment and competition in telecommunications. But it must also recognise that some commercial services can become matters of national security. When communications networks are used by the armed forces, emergency services and critical public institutions, their availability cannot be left entirely to commercial considerations. The controversy surrounding Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has brought this question into focus. Musk’s public clash with Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani is ostensibly about competition, market access and consumer choice. But the larger issue is whether India can afford to become excessively dependent on a critical communications network controlled by a foreign private company. Ukraine’s experience offers an important lesson. According to Reuters, Ukrainian military operations faced disruption in October after restrictions were imposed on satellite communications supporting drone missions. A Reuters report on October 15 said the reported order to limit access to the military-oriented Starshield system had come from within the White House. The service was subsequently restored following discussions between the US and British defence leadership. An important distinction must be made here. Starlink provides satellite broadband services, while Starshield is a separate, military-oriented system developed by SpaceX for government and defence applications. Nevertheless, the episode raises a serious question: what happens when a country becomes dependent on a communications network whose operations are controlled by a private company based abroad? The fact remains, Ukraine has benefited enormously from Starlink since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. The service helped keep hospitals, government offices and emergency services connected when conventional communications infrastructure was damaged. It also became important for military communications and drone operations. Starlink has played an important role in helping Ukraine withstand the crisis. But its recent experience also shows that over-reliance on a privately run network can pose a security risk when circumstances change. India needs to learn from this. It does not mean that Starlink is unsafe or that American technology should be avoided. The point is simple: no country should depend so heavily on a foreign-controlled communication network that its national security is at risk if that service is disrupted or restricted. India must have reliable alternatives of its own. Elon Musk has accused influential Indian business interests of trying to obstruct Starlink’s entry to protect their existing market positions. In a sarcastic remark, as national media reported, directed at Ambani, he used the expression “Prime Minister Ambani”, arguing that competition would give consumers more choices and encourage companies to offer better services at affordable prices. Reliance, in its October 16 statement, said it had never feared competition and welcomed satellite communications services, including Starlink. It also said its own satellite services were awaiting government clearances and maintained that Indian and foreign operators should be governed by the same rules. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said that three operators — Starlink, Reliance Jio’s satellite venture and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, have received licences, subject to the remaining requirements for commercial operations. There are important, legitimate questions about the pace of regulatory clearances and whether established companies are trying to protect their market positions. These issues should be examined on the basis of facts and transparent rules, rather than through public exchanges between wealthy businessmen. But the debate must not end there. Even if every allegation of commercial lobbying were proved wrong, New Delhi’s security concerns would and should remain. Similarly, even if Starlink offered the most attractive prices, affordability alone would not settle the question of strategic dependence. Satellite internet can bring benefits to a country as geographically diverse as India. It can connect remote Himalayan villages, islands, border settlements, ships and disaster-hit areas where laying fibre-optic cables is difficult or uneconomical. We agree that people living in remote regions need better connectivity to improve access to education, healthcare, banking and government services. Businesses can also benefit from more reliable communication. Starlink’s established technology and extensive satellite constellation could help expand connectivity in underserved areas. India should not deny these advantages merely because the service is foreign-owned. However, satellite networks differ from conventional telecom infrastructure. A terrestrial internet provider relies substantially on infrastructure located within the country. Satellite broadband depends on spacecraft in orbit, ground equipment, specialised terminals, software and a network operated by a company headquartered abroad. Indian authorities can regulate services offered within the country, but independently verifying every aspect of a complex satellite network presents a different challenge. The first concern is continuity of service. What would happen if a foreign operator restricted connectivity during a military confrontation, border emergency or diplomatic dispute? Would hospitals, emergency services and security agencies be able to continue their work? The second concern is data security. Satellite networks can generate information about users, terminals, locations and network activity. Some of this information may be commercially valuable, while other data could have security implications. India must establish enforceable safeguards governing the collection, storage, processing and sharing of such information. The most important issue is operational control and compliance with Indian law. It cannot be taken in a lighter way. Authorities, in all circumstances, should be able to address unlawful use, enforce legitimate restrictions and ensure that satellite services meet the country’s regulatory requirements. These safeguards become particularly important in sensitive border areas and strategically significant locations. These are genuine policy questions, not arguments for protectionism. The country should also not be dependent on a single point of dependence India’s digital transformation has made communications infrastructure essential to banking, commerce, public services, defence and disaster management. A disruption that once affected a limited number of users can now have consequences for entire systems. Consider a major earthquake, flood or other disaster that damages terrestrial networks. Satellite internet could become invaluable when conventional communication lines fail. But if the satellite service itself becomes unavailable, or its capacity is restricted at the very moment it is needed most, the country could face another crisis. The answer is not to reject satellite technology but to ensure that no single network becomes the only option. The same principle applies to national security. India cannot assume that a commercial service will remain available under every geopolitical circumstance. Equally, it should not presume that a foreign company will necessarily act against Indian interests. National planning must be based on safeguards and alternatives, rather than either assumption. This concern is not just about Elon Musk or the United States. The same questions would arise if a company from any other country controlled a communication network on which India depended for its critical needs. Allowing a foreign company to provide a service is one thing; depending on it for essential national functions is quite another. The first gives people more choices and improves connectivity. The second calls for much greater caution. India, now one of the leading global powers, should neither shut its doors to Starlink nor let a dispute between two business leaders decide the country’s technology policy. The government must encourage new technology and investment while ensuring that national interests are not compromised. First, there should be clear rules for all satellite service providers on data protection, security, access to information by lawful authorities and accountability. Indian and foreign companies should follow the same standards. Second, the government must ensure that essential communication services continue to work during emergencies. Defence establishments, disaster management agencies and other critical services should have access to alternative networks. These arrangements must also be tested regularly so that the country is not caught unprepared if one service is disrupted or restricted. Third, India needs to strengthen its own satellite technology and infrastructure. Indian companies and research institutions should get the support needed to develop local expertise and capabilities. Depending too much on a single foreign provider can limit the country’s options during a crisis. A mix of domestic and foreign services would give India greater flexibility. Finally, all decisions on satellite services must be foolproof and based on complete national security, technical needs and the public interest. They should not be influenced by pressure from technological giants, powerful business groups, or political considerations. Competition is important, but companies must also be held accountable for their services. Ukraine’s experience shows that technology can be a great help during a crisis, but it can also create new problems. A communication network that works well in normal times may become a source of concern when political relations change, or a conflict intensifies. The lesson for New Delhi is clear. India should neither shield domestic companies from competition nor reject foreign technology without reason. It must, however, ensure that dependence on any one company does not put the country at risk at a crucial moment: man-made or natural disaster. India should welcome new technology, guard completely against its risks and protect its strategic independence. Author is National Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: Nana Patekar: An Essayist of Characters
stories.title: Nana Patekar: An Essayist of Characters
stories.summary: Nana Patekar died in the early hours of Thursday, 8 October 2026 of a cardiac arrest at his home in Goa. He was seventy-five. Four days earlier, at a function near Panaji, he had spoken of death without theatre. “We all have to go someday. I don’t know whether I will be here tomorrow… But before the time comes… we have to think… am I able to do what I want to do? Have I made the effort?” Then, The Indian Express reports, he danced with a troupe and told a fan who asked for a Krantiveer dialogue that none would leave his throat until he heard the jingling of money in his ears. Frank, funny, faintly dangerous, and honest about the clock: that was Nana to the last. I keep a short roll of honour among the world’s actors: Gregory Peck, Marlon Brando, Robert De Niro, Al Pacino, Dilip Kumar, George C. Scott, Donald Sutherland, Sir Anthony Hopkins, Charles Chaplin, Alec Guinness, Jack Nicholson. Nana Patekar belongs on that roll, and not as a courtesy of nationality. He was an essayist of characters. Each of his men arrived as a thesis, made its case in a rasp or a silence, and left the audience altered. Look at the range. In Salaam Bombay! (1988) he was Baba, a drug dealer and pimp without a flicker of pity. In Parinda (1989) he was the crime lord Anna Seth, whose maniacal laugh won him his first National Award. In Krantiveer (1994) he turned anger into a public argument against corruption and won Best Actor. In Khamoshi: The Musical (1996) he played a deaf-mute father with no dialogue to lean on; the Express called it “pure performance, the hallmark of a true actor.” In Ab Tak Chhappan (2004) he was a police inspector “so obsessed with cleaning up crime that all semblance of balance disappeared.” In Natsamrat (2016) he became Ganpat “Appa” Belwalkar, the stage legend who neglected his family in his prime and found they had little time for him in old age. What I prize in the men on my roll is economy: a pause doing the work of a paragraph. Nana had it. His villains were never cartoons, and his heroes never forgot they were angry men. Honorary ranks are often treated as ornaments. Nana Patekar’s was not. He came to my Regiment first through a film. In Prahaar (1991), which he co-wrote, directed and starred in, he played Major Chavan of the Maratha Light Infantry, a hard taskmaster to his cadets. By several accounts he prepared by training with the Regiment for about three years. He joined the Territorial Army as an honorary Captain around 1990, and held his honorary commission, rising to Lieutenant Colonel, until 2013. Then came 1999. He asked to go to the front and was told that only the Defence Minister could permit it. So he telephoned George Fernandes, who agreed. He reached the Line of Control in August, weeks after the Kargil war was officially declared over, and did the unglamorous work: a base hospital, a quick-response team, patrols. He did not play at being a combatant. Kashmiri readers will know the places. By his own telling, his travels took in Dras, Leh, Kupwara, Baramulla and Sopore. I know that belt. Kupwara is my home district, and Baramulla is where I commanded my battalion on the Line of Control. “When I reached Srinagar, my weight was 76 kg,” he recalled. “When I came back, my weight became 56 kg.” In a recent interview he said of that time, simply: “I felt happy. I could at least do this little bit for the country.” That is how soldiers speak of service: without ornament. There is a coincidence I cannot leave alone. In 1978, the year I was commissioned into the 16th Battalion of the Maratha Light Infantry, Nana Patekar made his screen debut in Gaman . Two roads began that year, and they met in one Regiment. A regiment is a family of obligations. Whoever wears its uniform and means it, belongs to it. Nana meant it. He knew his own faults. “I get violent,” he told the Express in 2016. “That’s the difference. I lost so many things because of that.” Few public men name their flaw so plainly. In the same breath he said: “Acting is not just a profession for me. This is how I breathe.” His generosity was quieter than his temper. In 2015 he and Makarand Anaspure founded the NAAM Foundation to help drought-hit farmers and their families in Maharashtra. And when he learnt that the young shooter Anjali Bhagwat and two teammates were sharing one rifle and one kit for want of money, he stepped in. “He is the first sponsor of my career,” she says. To newcomers on the range he would say, on the spot: “Take my ammunition and shoot.” No glove? “Here, take mine. I’ll get a new one.” I must also set down a private regret. I have created and written a screenplay of an eight-episode feature for Netflix that marries Dostoevsky’s quiet pathos to the reckonings of love in King Lear . Its lead is an ageing patriarch who reeks of lust and greed. My sponsors offered a distinguished shortlist of the country’s finest actors. I insisted on Nana Patekar. My reason was what I call the Al Pacino frequency: volatile, razor-edged, soul-piercing. Nana had an innate, unpredictable savagery. In Parinda it announced itself. In Apaharan , as the MLA and underworld don Tabrez Alam, it learned to wait. Even in The Vaccine War , in a very different part, he kept his power in reserve. With age the fire had hardened into something more dangerous: a quiet, sardonic, bone-chilling cruelty. I wanted that savagery of intent dripping from my patriarch’s face and eyes before he spoke a word. I could not imagine another face carrying it. Every writer has a role written for one particular face. Mine was his. Now it is my loss, and a regret I will carry for life. He was cremated late on Thursday night at his farmhouse in Donje village, outside Pune, with full state honours and a 21-gun salute, before more than a thousand mourners. The salute fitted. He had worn two uniforms, the actor’s and the soldier’s, and neither was a disguise. Rest well, Colonel. The Regiment remembers you. Bol Shri Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj ki Jai. (The writer, a retired Colonel of the Maratha Light Infantry, is a strategic analyst and author.)

I keep a short roll of honour among the world’s actors: Gregory Peck, Marlon Brando, Robert De Niro, Al Pacino, Dilip Kumar, George C. Scott, Donald Sutherland, Sir Anthony Hopkins, Charles Chaplin, Alec Guinness, Jack Nicholson.
Nana Patekar belongs on that roll, and not as a courtesy of nationality.
He was an essayist of characters.
Each of his men arrived as a thesis, made its case in a rasp or a silence, and left the audience altered.
Look at the range.
In Salaam Bombay!
(1988) he was Baba, a drug dealer and pimp without a flicker of pity.
In Parinda (1989) he was the crime lord Anna Seth, whose maniacal laugh won him his first National Award.
In Krantiveer (1994) he turned anger into a public argument against corruption and won Best Actor.

In Khamoshi: The Musical (1996) he played a deaf-mute father with no dialogue to lean on; the Express called it “pure performance, the hallmark of a true actor.” In Ab Tak Chhappan (2004) he was a police inspector “so obsessed with cleaning up crime that all semblance of balance disappeared.” In Natsamrat (2016) he became Ganpat “Appa” Belwalkar, the stage legend who neglected his family in his prime and found they had little time for him in old age.
What I prize in the men on my roll is economy: a pause doing the work of a paragraph.
Nana had it.
His villains were never cartoons, and his heroes never forgot they were angry men.
Honorary ranks are often treated as ornaments.
Nana Patekar’s was not.
He came to my Regiment first through a film.
In Prahaar (1991), which he co-wrote, directed and starred in, he played Major Chavan of the Maratha Light Infantry, a hard taskmaster to his cadets.
By several accounts he prepared by training with the Regiment for about three years.
He joined the Territorial Army as an honorary Captain around 1990, and held his honorary commission, rising to Lieutenant Colonel, until 2013.
Then came 1999.
He asked to go to the front and was told that only the Defence Minister could permit it.
So he telephoned George Fernandes, who agreed.
He reached the Line of Control in August, weeks after the Kargil war was officially declared over, and did the unglamorous work: a base hospital, a quick-response team, patrols.
He did not play at being a combatant.
Kashmiri readers will know the places.
By his own telling, his travels took in Dras, Leh, Kupwara, Baramulla and Sopore.
I know that belt.
Kupwara is my home district, and Baramulla is where I commanded my battalion on the Line of Control.
“When I reached Srinagar, my weight was 76 kg,” he recalled.
“When I came back, my weight became 56 kg.” In a recent interview he said of that time, simply: “I felt happy.
I could at least do this little bit for the country.” That is how soldiers speak of service: without ornament.
There is a coincidence.
I cannot leave alone.
In 1978, the year.
I was commissioned into the 16th Battalion of the Maratha Light Infantry, Nana Patekar made his screen debut in Gaman.
Two roads began that year, and they met in one Regiment.
A regiment is a family of obligations.
Whoever wears its uniform and means it, belongs to it.
Nana meant it.
He knew his own faults.
“I get violent,” he told the Express in 2016.
“That’s the difference.
I lost so many things because of that.” Few public men name their flaw so plainly.
In the same breath he said: “Acting is not just a profession for me.
This is how I breathe.” His generosity was quieter than his temper.
In 2015 he and Makarand Anaspure founded the NAAM Foundation to help drought-hit farmers and their families in Maharashtra.
And when he learnt that the young shooter Anjali Bhagwat and two teammates were sharing one rifle and one kit for want of money, he stepped in.
“He is the first sponsor of my career,” she says.
To newcomers on the range he would say, on the spot: “Take my ammunition and shoot.” No glove?
“Here, take mine.
I’ll get a new one.” I must also set down a private regret.
I have created and written a screenplay of an eight-episode feature for Netflix that marries Dostoevsky’s quiet pathos to the reckonings of love in King Lear.
Its lead is an ageing patriarch who reeks of lust and greed.
My sponsors offered a distinguished shortlist of the country’s finest actors.
I insisted on Nana Patekar.
My reason was what I call the Al Pacino frequency: volatile, razor-edged, soul-piercing.
Nana had an innate, unpredictable savagery.
In Parinda it announced itself.
In Apaharan, as the MLA and underworld don Tabrez Alam, it learned to wait.
Even in The Vaccine War, in a very different part, he kept his power in reserve.
With age the fire had hardened into something more dangerous: a quiet, sardonic, bone-chilling cruelty.
I wanted that savagery of intent dripping from my patriarch’s face and eyes before he spoke a word.
I could not imagine another face carrying it.
Every writer has a role written for one particular face.
Mine was his.
Now it is my loss, and a regret.
I will carry for life.
He was cremated late on Thursday night at his farmhouse in Donje village, outside Pune, with full state honours and a 21-gun salute, before more than a thousand mourners.
The salute fitted.
He had worn two uniforms, the actor’s and the soldier’s, and neither was a disguise.
Rest well, Colonel.
The Regiment remembers you.
Bol Shri Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj ki Jai.
(The writer, a retired Colonel of the Maratha Light Infantry, is a strategic analyst and author.)

stories.title: CS Ladakh highlights infrastructure achievements, progress on constitutional safeguards for Ladakh
stories.summary: Kargil, Oct 17: A day after the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) rejected the Centre's draft proposal on Ladakh's demands, Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra on Saturday termed the response "very unfortunate", saying the document was dismissed within two hours of its receipt without its clauses being examined in depth. Addressing a press conference in Leh, Kundra said the draft had been prepared after considerable effort and was open to suggestions, stressing that the Centre was willing to consider changes to reach a consensus on constitutional safeguards and the proposed democratic structure for Ladakh. Chief Secretary described the successive meetings between Ladakh’s representatives and the MHA as constructive, with tangible progress towards addressing the aspirations of the people. He highlighted key measures already undertaken, including enhancement of Scheduled Tribe reservation to 84 per cent, recruitment of 107 local candidates against 109 Group A doctor posts through UPSC, recognition of Bhoti and Purgi as official languages, and one-third reservation for women in the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDCs). The Chief Secretary informed that, following discussions on October 15, the MHA shared a detailed framework document with Ladakh’s representatives on October 16. The document proposes a two-stage approach involving a constitutional amendment and a subsequent regulation under Article 240 of the Constitution, with provisions envisaged for a directly elected Union Territory-level body and safeguards concerning land, natural resources, culture and other issues raised by the representatives. He clarified that the document was intended to facilitate further discussion and was not the outcome of a concluded legislative process. The proposed constitutional provisions and the subsequent regulatory framework would require detailed examination and deliberation before being finalised. The Chief Secretary said that several institutional questions remained open for consideration and examination, including the nomenclature and composition of the proposed body, the method of election, representation of women and underrepresented communities, nominated and ex-officio members, the authority responsible for conducting elections, delimitation of constituencies, electoral rolls, tenure and the relationship of the proposed body with existing institutions such as the LAHDCs, Panchayats and municipalities. Reaffirming the Central Government’s commitment to the dialogue, the Chief Secretary said the objective was to arrive at a balanced and workable framework that reflects the democratic aspirations of the people while ensuring institutional clarity and taking into account its distinctive geographical, cultural and administrative circumstances through sustained dialogue and mutual understanding. The Chief Secretary emphasised that these issues could not be settled unilaterally and required broad-based consensus among the leadership and stakeholders of Ladakh. He urged all stakeholders to approach the process constructively and expressed hope that the remaining issues would be resolved through continued consultation in the coming weeks and months. The Chief Secretary, highlighted major infrastructure achievements dedicated to the people of Ladakh by the Prime Minister on October 15 and outlined the progress made in discussions with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on constitutional safeguards and the proposed democratic framework for the Union Territory. The Chief Secretary said that infrastructure projects worth approximately Rs 3,350 crore were dedicated to the people of Ladakh, with around 10,000 people from all seven districts participating virtually in the programme. Key highlights included the completion of the Leh Airport Terminal, valued at approximately ₹ 640 crore, with flight operations commencing on October 16; improved connectivity to Zanskar, reducing travel time from Leh from nearly 12 hours to approximately three hours; and the commissioning of the 9 MW Hanu Hydropower Project, taking the combined capacity of the Dha and Hanu projects to 18 MW. Emphasising water conservation, the Chief Secretary stated that, in response to public demand, the Lieutenant Governor had directed an increase in the number of Amrit Sarovars from 40 to 100 across Ladakh. He also highlighted the Petroglyph Park along the Indus as an important initiative for preserving and showcasing the region’s rich archaeological heritage and historical links with the Silk Route. The Chief Secretary also highlighted the establishment of the High Court Bench in Leh as a significant milestone in improving access to justice in Ladakh. The presence of the Chief Justice and Judges of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, along with the Attorney General of India, underscored the importance of the occasion. He noted that the initiative, operationalised within a span of two months, would significantly ease access to High Court services for the people of Ladakh by reducing the need to travel to Jammu or Srinagar. He described it as a proactive initiative of the Government of India, reflecting its sensitivity to Ladakh’s geographical challenges and commitment to bringing justice closer to the people.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court has directed all States and Union Territories to take steps to confer police station status on Anti-Human Trafficking Units (ATHUs) by issuing appropriate notifications in accordance with law, emphasising that the measure is necessary for the effective implementation of its Victim Protection Plan to combat human trafficking.
A bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice R. Mahadevan directed the Home Departments of all States and Union Territories to give effect to the direction at the earliest.
It also asked the Union Government to take up the issue with all States and UTs and ensure that the necessary notifications are issued.

The direction came during an ongoing hearing in which the Court reviewed compliance with its May 29, 2026 judgment concerning human trafficking of women and children for commercial sexual exploitation.

Senior Advocate Aparna Bhat, appearing for the petitioner, brought to the Court's attention that ATHUs needed to be given the status of police stations in accordance with paragraph 362(b)(iii) of the main judgment.

“In this regard, we direct all the State/UT Governments in their respective Home Departments to give effect to this direction at the earliest by issuing an appropriate notification, in accordance with law.”
The Court added that the Union Government “shall also take up this issue at the earliest with all the States/UTs and see to it that appropriate notifications are issued.”
The direction forms part of the Court's broader effort to ensure effective implementation of the Victim Protection Plan framed under Article 142 of the Constitution.
The bench noted that the four additional directions issued in paragraph 456 of its main judgment had not been fully complied with by all States and UTs.

These include notifying recognised welfare institutions under Sections 15(6A) and 17A of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956; preparing State- and UT-wide lists of eligible social welfare workers; and designating.

stories.title: Supreme Court grants bail to former Rajasthan Minister in Jal Jeevan Mission case
stories.summary: The Justices ordered the release of Mukesh Pathak, another accused, setting aside an August 13 order of the Rajasthan High Court denying regular bail
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court of India granted bail on Friday (October 16, 2026) to former Congress Minister Mahesh Joshi in connection with the alleged Jal Jeevan Mission scam, observing that prolonged pre-trial detention cannot be allowed to “degenerate into punishment without trial” in breach of constitutional guarantees.

A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu also ordered the release of Mukesh Pathak, another accused in the case, setting aside an August 13 order of the Rajasthan High Court denying them regular bail.

“There can be no gainsaying that allegations of large-scale financial impropriety and institutional collusion in the execution of a public welfare project such as the ‘Jal Jeevan Mission’ are grave and warrant serious scrutiny.
We think the State is justified in opposing the grant of bail to persons accused of involvement in such extensive criminal activity.

Nevertheless, the gravity of the allegations, however serious, cannot by itself eclipse all other considerations governing the grant of bail or justify indefinite pre-trial detention,” the Bench said.
The court noted that the investigation against both accused was complete and chargesheets had been filed.
The prosecution's case rests overwhelmingly on documentary and electronic evidence already in the investigating agency’s custody.
It added that the possibility of tampering with such evidence had been “substantially obviated” and that neither accused was required for further custodial interrogation or recovery.
The case stems from an Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) probe into alleged irregularities in tenders floated by Rajasthan’s Public Health Engineering Department (PHED) under the Jal Jeevan Mission.

According to the prosecution, two firms participated in 237 tenders between 2021 and 2023 using forged work completion certificates and letters of acceptance purportedly issued by IRCON International Limited.
The firms allegedly emerged as the lowest bidders on the strength of these credentials and secured work orders in 104 tenders worth a combined ₹979.45 crore.
The Bench noted that the case involves 22 accused, three chargesheets, 124 prosecution witnesses, and 20,000 pages of documents.

Her family has accused her husband and mother-in-law of mental harassment and making financial demands.

stories.headline: The growing burden of cancer drugs
stories.title: The growing burden of cancer drugs
stories.summary: Six months ago, Surekha Panicker (name changed), a 65-year-old retired professional from Kerala, stared at her diagnosis in shock—stage-2 breast cancer. She had no family and limited savings. She went to an oncologist at a leading private hospital to figure out a treatment plan. They decided on immunotherapy, particularly Roche’s injection Phesgo, which would cost Rs 5 lakh for the first loading dose of a 1,200 mg vial and over Rs 2 lakh for subsequent doses. She was offered a “buy one, get one” deal under Roche’s patient assistance programme— you pay for one cycle and the next will be free. She was prescribed eight cycles.After two cycles, Panicker developed a severe bacterial infection and had to pause the treatment and go for surgery. The free offer lapsed due to the break. She has paid over Rs 35 lakh from her own pocket—for the treatment of the infection, the surgery, all subsequent cycles of immunotherapy and other hospital charges. Her funds are almost exhausted. Panicker doesn’t know how to pay for another course of treatment.Also Read: NPPA caps trade margins on 137 cancer drugs at 30%, revised prices from Nov 9“My husband died two decades ago. I have no kids or close relatives. I spent my savings on immunotherapy in the hope that it would buy me at least 10 years. I don’t know how I will manage if I need to continue the treatment,” says Panicker.135023376It is not just Panicker’s plight. opening: Six months ago, Surekha Panicker (name changed), a 65-year-old retired professional from Kerala, stared at her diagnosis in shock—stage-2 breast cancer.
She had no family and limited savings.
body: She went to an oncologist at a leading private hospital to figure out a treatment plan.
They decided on immunotherapy, particularly Roche’s injection Phesgo, which would cost Rs 5 lakh for the first loading dose of a 1,200 mg vial and over Rs 2 lakh for subsequent doses.
She was offered a “buy one, get one” deal under Roche’s patient assistance programme— you pay for one cycle and the next will be free.
She was prescribed eight cycles.
After two cycles, Panicker developed a severe bacterial infection and had to pause the treatment and go for surgery.
The free offer lapsed due to the break.
She has paid over Rs 35 lakh from her own pocket—for the treatment of the infection, the surgery, all subsequent cycles of immunotherapy and other hospital charges.
Her funds are almost exhausted.
Panicker doesn’t know how to pay for another course of treatment.
“My husband died two decades ago.
I have no kids or close relatives.
I spent my savings on immunotherapy in the hope that it would buy me at least 10 years.
I don’t know how I will manage if I need to continue the treatment,” says Panicker.
It is not just Panicker’s plight.
Millions of cancer patients in India have to bear the double burden of the disease and the dreadfully expensive treatment.
A PRESCRIPTION AWAY FROM BANKRUPTCYThe high cost of cancer drugs is in full public glare after the Supreme Court criticised the massive markup in their prices.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, hearing two writ petitions filed by lawyer Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surge on Sanjay Kulshrestha, said medicines that are purchased by retailers for Rs 2,700 are being sold to patients for Rs 27,000.
They called it “broad daylight dacoity”.
The anger of the bench resonates with the people.
In a country where 1.5 million cancer cases are detected every year, a diagnosis very often leads to a long painful road of financial distress.
Patients drain bank accounts, wipe out savings and even sell land just to get their hands on these promising but prohibitively expensive new medicines.
How did India fail to make life-saving drugs affordable for its population?
A Mumbai-based oncologist says the situation is dire.
“People are only a prescription away from bankruptcy,” he says.

Patients have no hope in the absence of a fair pricing mechanism, a pooled procurement plan by hospital networks and an effective insurance and reimbursement system, he says on condition of anonymity.
There are exceptions though.
The Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai procures drugs on a negotiated model, at rates that are far less than the maximum retail price (MRP), which makes them cheaper for its patients.

A study by top oncologists published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2023 showed that a pooled procurement of 40 drugs by the National Cancer Grid—a network of over 250 cancer centres—saved `13.2 billion compared with MRP.
The savings ranged from 23% to 99%.
COST OF CARETop private hospitals do not agree that they are committing medical dacoity.
In addition to the retail price of the medicine, they say, the hospital bill includes the cost of administration, use of facility, storage, training and consumables.
Abhay Soi, chairman and managing director of Max Healthcare Institute, says at the end of the day, a hospital is not selling an IV fluid bag.
“A hospital is administering an injection.
There is a particular training, a particular storage requirement, the administration of medicine and then the disposal through proper biomedical waste processes.
There is an entire value chain,” he says.
Hospitals have thousands of individual billing items, with margins varying across products and services, he says.
“Some won’t have a margin, some will have a margin.
Ultimately, it translates to 8-9% net profit,” says Soi.
He says hospital profitability needs to be viewed against the sector’s capital intensity and continuing investment requirements.
“Your equipment gets totally depreciated.
You replace the entire equipment every 10 years.
Eventually, you must reinvest as well,” he says.
BS Ajai Kumar, founder of specialty cancer hospital group HCG Enterprises, backs Soi’s point.
He says it is important to understand that India provides high-quality cancer treat ment at a much lower cost than many Western countries like US.
Private hospitals, he adds, should be assessed not simply by the markup on an individual drug but the overall cost of treatment relative to the quality of care and outcomes delivered.
THE MARKUPSHealth activists, however, note that hospitals lack transparency.
They ask: what is the chain of markups from pharma manufacturers to distribution chains and healthcare providers?
In response to the Supreme Court’s criticism, the government has proposed a cap on trade margins for non-scheduled cancer drugs, which are not listed in Drugs (Prices Control) Order or DPCO.
The margin is proposed to be capped at 30% of MRP.
This means drug purchased for Rs700 cannot be sold for more than Rs 1,000.
The move, the government says, could bring down prices by up to 70% and can help patients save Rs 2,500 crore annually.
However, civil society and patient advocacy groups are not sure of the impact of this intervention.
Several stakeholders, including doctors, told ET that the larger issue remains unresolved and several drugs, specifically patented drugs, are still exorbitantly priced.
“Patient assistance programmes of MNCs, though well-intentioned, are not adequate,” says a health activist.
“High base prices, steep hospital markups and limited disclosure of procurement costs are behind the problem,” says Jain, who moved the petition in the apex court.
There is a huge difference in the prices of some cancer drugs sold through the Jan Aushadhi Scheme, the government’s fair price stores, and other retail shops, claims Jain’s petition.
A 50 mg vial of doxorubicin injection costs Rs 250 at Jan Aushadhi, while the average price of top three brands for the same medicine in other retail shops is Rs 1,230 —an increase of over 390%.
Jain says trade margin for drugs should be calculated on the actual exfactory price or purchase price rather than as a percentage of printed MRP.
A medicine purchased for Rs 700 can be given an MRP of Rs 1,000 under the new trade margin cap proposed by the government.
But that markup of Rs 300 is still about 43% of the purchase price.
DIFFERENT PROBLEMSExperts say the proposed margin cap of 30% will have an effect on drugs with exceptionally high markups.
However,it will have little impact on patented cancer drugs that cost Rs 1.5-2 lakh for a vial and tens of thousands of rupees for a strip of tablets as their prices are not pushed up by markups.

Multinational companies supply their patented medicines based on a combination of factors—the country’s population and expected demand, international reference pricing, per capita income and paying or purchasing capacity of the country.
“For patented medicines, margin capping does not work.

And in the case of generic medicines, the regulation may not work on every drug,” says KM Gopakumar, co-con vener, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treat-ments, a network of patients and activists fighting for affordable healthcare.
He says there should be a clear distinction between excessive hospital-level markups and high cost of patented drugs.
The two problems may require different regulatory interventions.
Gopakumar cites a public interest litigation on the high cost of the breast cancer drug ribociclib.
It cost Rs 78,000 for a month’s treatment before 2019 when the government regulated the prices of 42 cancer drugs.
Ribociclib’s price has come down but it is still unaffordable at Rs 66,000.
TAXING MRPAbhay Shukla, co-convener of Jan Swasthya Abhiyan, a national network on public health, also says markups will have limited impact.
He says all cancer medicines should be brought under the scheduled price-control framework.
“Drug prices must be determined by production costs rather than inflated market prices,” he says.

“Regulators should first establish a medicine’s production cost and use that as the basis for determining a reasonable price, rather than rely on the prices charged by manufacturers.” That may not be easy.
Global drug firms price their new innovations based on comparable benefits over available treatment options and cost of research which runs into billions of dollars.
Shukla says pharmaceutical companies often print inflated MRPs and offer hospitals substantial discounts while hospitals sell the medicine to patients at the printed price.
“Controlling the margins of hospitals alone does not address the problem if the MRP itself is inflated,” he says.

Besides, he says, DPCO covers only a fraction of the drug market, leaving a significant part—which includes many high-cost, life-saving drugs—outside the purview of direct price regulation or ceiling.
The manufacturers of non-scheduled medicines can determine the launch price, but subsequent increases cannot exceed more than 10% annually.
The apex court has questioned the Centre on restricting price control to select cancer medicines, asking why similar measures are not being considered for other drugs.
Jain estimates that extending price reduction across the broader non-scheduled market could potentially save patients around Rs 1 lakh crore annually.
“Profit should not mean profiteering,” he says.
The debate has spilled over, with even hospitals and medical insurance companies sparring over reimbursement rates.
Top insurers are pushing for a regulatory mechanism for greater standardisation of hospital pricing and treatment protocols.
Mayank Bathwal, CEO of Aditya Birla Health Insurance, says: “We don’t have a health regulator as it is a state subject.

There must be a mechanism for regulation of healthcare services and pricing within certain norms so that whoever is investing is getting a fair return but, most importantly, consumers are provided affordable healthcare services.” The Supreme Court has set in motion a much-needed debate on affordable cancer care.
But patients like Panicker have a finite waiting time.
They need a treatment within their means soon.
The cost of remission should not be harrowing debt.
